item.title: Is Their Water Bowl Hiding a Surprising Upgrade?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Hydrogen water is regular water infused with dissolved molecular hydrogen gas, the smallest molecule in existence, which acts as a selective antioxidant that neutralizes only the most damaging free radicals without disrupting normal cell function
  • A 2021 study in beagles found dogs drinking hydrogen-rich water healed wounds in 19 days versus 22 days for controls, with better tissue vascularization and elevated antioxidant enzyme activity
  • Research and integrative veterinary practice point to potential benefits for wound healing, joint comfort, cognitive support in senior pets, gut health, coat quality, and athletic recovery in active dogs
  • Recommended starting doses are 1 to 2 milliliters (ml) per kilogram daily for dogs and 0.5 to 1 ml per kilogram for cats, introduced gradually alongside regular water rather than replacing it entirely
  • Skip or check with a vet first for pets undergoing chemotherapy, on diuretics, with congestive heart failure, immediately post-surgery, under eight weeks old, or cats with chronic kidney disease

You've done the research on pet food. You've thought about supplements. You've even upgraded to a nicer stainless-steel dish. But have you ever given a thought to the water going into their bowl?

Most pet parents haven't given it a second thought beyond using filtered water. And yet a small but growing body of veterinary and integrative health research suggests there's a surprisingly simple upgrade happening in some kitchens right now — one that might do more for your pet's joints, healing, and even aging brain than most of the pricier supplements on the shelf.

What Hydrogen Water Actually Is

Hydrogen water is regular water (H₂O) with additional dissolved molecular hydrogen gas (H₂), which is the smallest molecule in existence. Not to be confused with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), which is toxic, molecular hydrogen is an odorless, colorless, nontoxic gas that dissolves into water and behaves as a selective antioxidant once inside the body.

The therapeutic range studied in animals is roughly 0.5 to 1.6 parts per million (500 to 1,600 parts per billion) of dissolved H₂. What makes it interesting is how the molecule behaves in the body. Because it's so small, it slips through cellular membranes and can reach places where most conventional antioxidants can't, including the mitochondria, cell nuclei, and even brain tissue.

And rather than neutralizing every free radical in sight (which can cause its own problems), molecular hydrogen selectively scavenges the most damaging reactive oxygen species, specifically hydroxyl radicals and peroxynitrite, while leaving the beneficial signaling oxidation processes alone. Excess hydrogen simply exhales out through the lungs.1,2

Why Antioxidants Matter for Your Pet

Dogs and cats live in the same environmental soup we do. They breathe the same indoor air, walk on treated lawns, share exposure to household chemicals, and eat processed foods that generate reactive oxygen species during metabolism. Their built-in antioxidant defenses — enzymes like superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase — gradually weaken with age.

That imbalance between free radicals and antioxidant capacity is what scientists call oxidative stress, and it's implicated in almost every chronic condition in aging pets: arthritis, cognitive decline, cardiovascular changes, cancer, kidney disease, and more.3,4

Anything that can gently support the body's antioxidant systems over the years your pet is with you is worth understanding. Hydrogen water is one of the more scientifically grounded options in the current pet wellness space.

What Research Actually Shows

The most rigorous pet-specific study on hydrogen water to date came out in 2021 in the journal Veterinary Sciences. Researchers worked with twelve male beagle dogs, created standardized skin wounds, and gave one group four hundred milliliters (ml) of hydrogen-rich water three times daily while the control group drank standard distilled water.5

The results were meaningful across every metric. The dogs drinking hydrogen water healed their wounds in an average of 19 days versus 22 days for the control group. At the 7-day mark, wound closure was 46.8% in the hydrogen group versus just 16.4% in the control group.

The tissue under a microscope showed significantly greater blood vessel density, which is what healing tissues need for oxygen and nutrient delivery. Biochemically, hydrogen water raised levels of SOD (superoxide dismutase) — an important antioxidant enzyme — and lowered markers of oxidative damage. It also activated the Nrf2 signaling pathway, which upregulates the body's own antioxidant defenses. And no adverse effects were reported throughout the study.6

Beyond that specific study, a large body of animal research — including hundreds of studies reviewed in a 2024 comprehensive review in Biochemistry and Biophysics Reports — supports molecular hydrogen's anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects across multiple mammalian systems.7 Studies in rodent models have shown reductions in hippocampal oxidative stress, improved cognitive performance in age-related decline, reduced markers of periodontal (gum and dental) damage, and reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6.8

Where the Benefits May Show Up in Your Pet

Based on the current research, hydrogen water may support a surprisingly wide range of everyday pet health concerns. The common thread across almost all of them is the same mechanism — reducing oxidative stress and calming low-grade inflammation before they can start to compound over the years.

  • Wound healing and post-surgical recovery — The strongest pet-specific research evidence links hydrogen water to faster wound closure and better tissue regeneration.9
  • Joint comfort and mobility — Molecular hydrogen's anti-inflammatory action may reduce the oxidative damage that drives arthritis and stiffness in aging dogs and cats.10
  • Cognitive support in senior pets — Canine Cognitive Dysfunction Syndrome affects roughly 28% of dogs aged 11 to 12 and over 68% of dogs aged 15 to 16. Hydrogen's ability to cross the blood-brain barrier and reduce oxidative stress in brain tissue is why some integrative vets believe that hydrogen may have healing potential for CCD.11
  • Gut health and immune support — Reduced intestinal oxidative stress and modulated immune responses — may be potentially relevant for pets with inflammatory bowel disease or food sensitivities.12
  • Coat and skin quality — The connection between oxidative stress and skin barrier function makes this a biologically plausible benefit, though controlled studies specifically on coat and skin health are lacking.13
  • Athletic recovery for active dogs — Studies on performance animals — including horses in competitive racing — have shown reduced muscle inflammation and lower blood lactate levels after intense exercise.14
  • Quality of life in older pets — Reduced anxiety, better mood, and improved nerve function have all been noted in human studies, and integrative vets increasingly extrapolate these to aging pets.15

How to Actually Give It

Introducing hydrogen water is simple, but a few practical notes matter — mostly because dissolved hydrogen behaves a little differently than any other supplement you might offer, and small mistakes in preparation or delivery can cancel out most of the benefits.

  • Start low, go slow — A conservative starting dose for dogs is 1 to 2 ml per kilogram of body weight per day. For cats, 0.5 to 1 ml per kilogram. Introduce it at about 25% of the target amount and build up over one to two weeks. Watch for any digestive changes as your pet adjusts.16
  • Don't replace all their water — Hydrogen water supplements the normal water bowl rather than replacing it entirely. This is especially important for cats, who can be stressed by abrupt changes to their drinking environment. Many pet parents offer hydrogen water in a separate bowl alongside their regular water and let their cat decide.
  • Fresh is best — Dissolved hydrogen begins off-gassing immediately after production. At room temperature in an open bowl, most of it dissipates within 30 to 60 minutes. Prepare hydrogen water close to serving time and offer it right after generating. In sealed containers, it holds for a few hours.
  • Morning delivery works well — Giving hydrogen water on an empty stomach in the morning appears to support the best absorption.
  • Monitor — Mild, temporary increases in urination can happen as the body responds to the antioxidant support. That's usually not a concern. Persistent digestive upset warrants discontinuing use and checking with your vet.

Choosing a Device Worth Trusting

Not all hydrogen water products are created equal. The quality of the technology directly affects how much dissolved hydrogen your pet receives and whether harmful byproducts get in along the way. Here are factors to look for:

  • Solid Polymer Electrolyte/Proton Exchange Membrane (SPE/PEM) technology — SPE/PEM electrolysis separates the electrolysis cell so that ozone and chlorine (toxic byproducts produced at the anode) are drained away separately. Single-chamber devices cannot separate these contaminants.
  • Platinum-coated titanium electrodes — This is the industry standard. They don't corrode, don't leach metals, and maintain consistent hydrogen production over time.
  • Verified PPB output — The device should specify its output in parts per billion or parts per million, ideally verified by independent laboratory testing rather than just manufacturer claims.
  • Third-party certifications — Look for International Hydrogen Standards Association (IHSA) certification and H₂ Analytics testing.
  • FDA-registered manufacturing facilities — are recommended for the device components that contact water.

Portable hydrogen water bottles work well for daily use and for taking on hikes or trips. Countertop pitchers or jugs are convenient for multi-pet households or families who also drink hydrogen water themselves. Regular carbon filters and reverse osmosis systems do not produce hydrogen water — you need a specific device that generates and dissolves molecular hydrogen. Hydrogen tablets exist too but tend to produce less predictable concentrations.17

When to Skip It or Ask Your Vet First

Hydrogen water has a strong safety profile, and no serious adverse events have been reported across human or animal studies. But there are situations that warrant extra caution or veterinary conversation before introducing it:18

  • Pets undergoing chemotherapy — Hydrogen's antioxidant effects could theoretically interfere with the effectiveness of chemotherapy. Talk to your veterinary oncologist first.
  • Pets on diuretic medications — Any increase in fluid intake could alter dosing or hydration status.
  • Pets with congestive heart failure — Increased fluid intake can be harmful for heart failure cases, so monitor your pet closely.
  • Immediately post-major surgery — Although it assists in wound healing, contact your vet to make sure it is safe for your pet’s particular surgery.
  • Young animals (under eight weeks) — Puppies and kittens should stick with species-appropriate milk or plain water during this window.
  • Cats with chronic kidney disease — May benefit from hydrogen water's antioxidant support (since oxidative stress drives CKD progression), but reduced fluid intake can be harmful for cats with kidney disease so monitor your pet closely.

For all pets, an integrative or holistic veterinarian who's familiar with hydrogen therapy is the best person to help decide whether it makes sense for your specific animal, especially if they are on medications or have chronic health conditions.

Honest Limits of the Science

It would be misleading to present hydrogen water as fully established therapy. The evidence base is promising but still developing. However, it’s worth acknowledging that most animal research has been short-term — days to weeks rather than years. Long-term multi-year safety data specifically in cats and dogs is still lacking.

Species-specific dosing standards haven't been formally published by major veterinary associations yet. Condition-specific efficacy trials in dogs and cats — for arthritis, IBD, CKD, cognitive decline — are limited compared to the human literature. And some of the more enthusiastic claims in the online pet wellness space run ahead of what the evidence supports currently.

None of that means hydrogen water is ineffective. The scientific evidence is solid, the safety data is reassuring, and the 2021 study provides real proof of concept. But it does mean hydrogen water should be viewed as a supportive tool in a comprehensive wellness plan — not a stand-alone treatment for diagnosed disease. Your pet's diet, their environment, their exercise, and their overall care all matter more than any single supplement, including this one.

What to Watch For

Since pets can't tell you how they feel, watch for these signals over four to eight weeks of consistent use:

  • Increased energy or playfulness, especially in senior pets
  • Reduced stiffness after sleep or rest
  • Improved coat sheen and less dry, flaky skin
  • More regular digestion
  • Calmer demeanor in anxious pets
  • Faster healing of minor cuts, scrapes, or post-operative incisions

If you see no meaningful change after eight to 12 weeks of consistent, properly dosed use, hydrogen water may simply not be the right intervention for your specific pet, and that's useful information too.19

The Real Takeaway

Water is the one thing your pet drinks every single day of their life. That daily volume over their lifetime, adds up to a big opportunity to deliver something beneficial through a simple intervention. Hydrogen water represents one of the more scientifically grounded ways to make that daily bowl of water do a little more work — supporting antioxidant defenses, calming inflammation, and helping tissues heal a little faster.

It's not a miracle and it is not a replacement for a good diet, regular holistic vet care, exercise, or the many other pieces of a well-rounded wellness plan. But for aging pets dealing with joint stiffness or cognitive changes, active dogs needing better recovery, or pets healing from surgery or injury, it's a low-risk addition that a growing number of integrative and holistic veterinarians are watching closely. The research is still evolving. The safety profile is reassuring. And the setup is genuinely as simple as swapping a bottle of water.

Your pet's water bowl has been sitting quietly on the kitchen floor for years. It might be time to take a second look at what's actually in it.

  • 2,3,10,14,17 Ion Bottles, April 1, 2026
  • 4,15 Rallie, April 1, 2022
  • 5,6,9 Vet Sci. 2021 Nov 4;8(11):264
  • 7 Biochem Biophys Rep. 2025 Jan 25;41:101933. doi: 10.1016/j.bbrep.2025.101933
  • 11 Curr Alzheimer Res. 2018 Mar 14;15(5):482-492

item.title: Senior Pit Bull Finds Someone to Love Her Again
item.description:
After her owner passed away, this senior pit bull traveled across the country looking for a new home. Her new mom fell in love with her instantly, and together they learned to trust each other. Now, she's a cuddly little shadow who even has Grandma and Grandpa wrapped around her paw.

item.title: Cube Steak Biscotti: A Decadent Treat for Your Precious Pets
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Cube Steak Biscotti is made from cube steak and fresh marjoram or rosemary
  • Beef is a high-quality source of species-appropriate protein and fats while marjoram provides flavor, vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants
  • Choose organic, grass fed beef instead of grain-fed to increase the level of vitamins, minerals and healthy fats
  • Cube steak is a tougher, more economical cut that is tenderized to make it more palatable, so it’s a budget-friendly way to feed grass fed beef
  • Fresh rosemary is also an excellent option for these treats, and there’s no reason to fear it causes seizures in pets

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published July 23, 2015.

Most pets will salivate at the sight of a beef cubed steak, especially one that’s meant just for them. If you want to pamper your pooch or your kitty with a special treat that’s deceptively simple to make (just two ingredients!), cube steak biscotti is it.

What makes this treat so appealing is what it doesn’t contain. You’ll find no fillers, no unnecessary grains and starches, no byproducts, no preservatives and no artificial anything ... just real meat and marjoram — a perennial herb similar to oregano but with a slightly sweeter flavor.

Cube Steak Biscotti Recipe

Ingredients:

  • One cube steak, sliced into strips
  • Three sprigs fresh marjoram or rosemary (pictured)

Directions:

  1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F
  2. Grease a slotted pizza pan
  3. Press fresh herb leaves into cubed steak strips
  4. Bake for 20 minutes
  5. Flip over and bake another 15 to 20 minutes until crispy
  6. Let cool thoroughly
  7. Store in airtight container in the freezer for up to three months

The Benefits of Feeding Your Pets Grass Fed Organic Beef

Beef, especially when it’s grass fed and organic, is an ideal treat for dogs and cats, providing a high-quality source of species-appropriate protein and fats. It's important to recognize that while the USDA 100% Organic label is good, it's not necessarily a guarantee that the meat has been grass fed and finished (rather it’s an indication the meat is free of synthetic pesticides and hormones).

The latter, grass fed, is likely even more important than organic, however, because when cows are raised on their natural diet of grass it changes the nutritional content of the meat considerably. A joint effort between the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and Clemson University researchers determined a total of 10 key areas where grass fed beef is better than grain-fed beef. Grass fed beef was determined to be:1

  • Lower in total fat
  • Higher in beta-carotene
  • Higher in vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol)
  • Higher in the B vitamins thiamin and riboflavin
  • Higher in the minerals calcium, magnesium and potassium
  • Higher in total omega-3s
  • A healthier ratio of omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acids (1.65 vs 4.84)
  • Higher in conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), a potential cancer fighter
  • Higher in vaccenic acid (which can be transformed into CLA)

If you’re worried about the cost of grass fed beef, cube steak tends to be a more economical choice. Since it’s a tougher cut of meat, the steak is cubed, or tenderized, to make it more palatable, and when prepared correctly it’s excellent. You may even remember eating cube steak yourself as a kid (it’s a popular type of meat for making Swiss steak, Salisbury steak and chicken-fried steak).

Marjoram or Rosemary: Why It’s a Perfect Addition to Pet Treats

Marjoram is closely related to oregano and shares many of the same health benefits for your pet. When choosing marjoram, look for “sweet marjoram,” as “wild marjoram” is often oregano.

True marjoram has a milder, sweeter flavor than oregano and is packed with antioxidants and vitamins. Marjoram is an anti-inflammatory herb, making it useful for lowering the risk of chronic diseases.

It’s also beneficial for heart health, helping to lower blood pressure, and improve circulation, and is said to have digestive benefits, including improving digestive efficiency by increasing digestive enzymes and saliva.2

Also to marjoram’s credit are antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral properties, and it even has mild sedative properties, which is why it’s sometimes recommended to help relieve stress and anxiety.

Not to mention, many pets enjoy the flavor of marjoram, and the extra “dose” of vitamins (including vitamins A, C, and K), minerals (iron, calcium, potassium, manganese, magnesium, and zinc), and antioxidants (beta-carotene, zeaxanthin, lutein, and more) are just the icing on the proverbial cake.

Fresh rosemary is also an excellent option to use in these homemade treats (as pictured). Unfortunately, rosemary has come under undo fire in the last 15 years since it’s been a common addition to pet foods as a natural preservative. Human literature states people with epilepsy should avoid high levels of rosemary oil, and this has translated into pet parents assuming this amazing herb causes seizures, which is absolutely does not.

Not only is there no reason to fear giving this medicinal herb to your pets, it’s a wonderful all-natural source of iron, calcium, and vitamin B6, which is critical for healthy neurologic wellbeing.

Really, very few store-bought treats can compare to the nutrition and flavor found in homemade pet treats. Your pets will certainly adore you for making them, and they make thoughtful gifts for your pet-loving friends and family too.  

Sources and References

  • 1 J ANIM SCI September 2009 Vol. 87 No. 9 2961-2970 (Archived)
  • 2 Herb Knowledge, Marjoram

  • Cube steak is a tougher, more economical cut that is tenderized to make it more palatable, so it’s a budget-friendly way to feed grass fed beef
  • Fresh rosemary is also an excellent option for these treats, and there’s no reason to fear it causes seizures in pets

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published July 23, 2015.

Most pets will salivate at the sight of a beef cubed steak, especially one that’s meant just for them. If you want to pamper your pooch or your kitty with a special treat that’s deceptively simple to make (just two ingredients!), cube steak biscotti is it.

What makes this treat so appealing is what it doesn’t contain. You’ll find no fillers, no unnecessary grains and starches, no byproducts, no preservatives and no artificial anything ... just real meat and marjoram — a perennial herb similar to oregano but with a slightly sweeter flavor.

Cube Steak Biscotti Recipe

Ingredients:

  • One cube steak, sliced into strips
  • Three sprigs fresh marjoram or rosemary (pictured)

Directions:

  1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F
  2. Grease a slotted pizza pan
  3. Press fresh herb leaves into cubed steak strips
  4. Bake for 20 minutes
  5. Flip over and bake another 15 to 20 minutes until crispy
  6. Let cool thoroughly
  7. Store in airtight container in the freezer for up to three months

The Benefits of Feeding Your Pets Grass Fed Organic Beef

Beef, especially when it’s grass fed and organic, is an ideal treat for dogs and cats, providing a high-quality source of species-appropriate protein and fats. It's important to recognize that while the USDA 100% Organic label is good, it's not necessarily a guarantee that the meat has been grass fed and finished (rather it’s an indication the meat is free of synthetic pesticides and hormones).

The latter, grass fed, is likely even more important than organic, however, because when cows are raised on their natural diet of grass it changes the nutritional content of the meat considerably. A joint effort between the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and Clemson University researchers determined a total of 10 key areas where grass fed beef is better than grain-fed beef. Grass fed beef was determined to be:1

  • Lower in total fat
  • Higher in beta-carotene
  • Higher in vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol)
  • Higher in the B vitamins thiamin and riboflavin
  • Higher in the minerals calcium, magnesium and potassium
  • Higher in total omega-3s
  • A healthier ratio of omega-6 to omega-3 fatty acids (1.65 vs 4.84)
  • Higher in conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), a potential cancer fighter
  • Higher in vaccenic acid (which can be transformed into CLA)

If you’re worried about the cost of grass fed beef, cube steak tends to be a more economical choice. Since it’s a tougher cut of meat, the steak is cubed, or tenderized, to make it more palatable, and when prepared correctly it’s excellent. You may even remember eating cube steak yourself as a kid (it’s a popular type of meat for making Swiss steak, Salisbury steak and chicken-fried steak).

Marjoram or Rosemary: Why It’s a Perfect Addition to Pet Treats

Marjoram is closely related to oregano and shares many of the same health benefits for your pet. When choosing marjoram, look for “sweet marjoram,” as “wild marjoram” is often oregano.

True marjoram has a milder, sweeter flavor than oregano and is packed with antioxidants and vitamins. Marjoram is an anti-inflammatory herb, making it useful for lowering the risk of chronic diseases.

It’s also beneficial for heart health, helping to lower blood pressure, and improve circulation, and is said to have digestive benefits, including improving digestive efficiency by increasing digestive enzymes and saliva.2

Also to marjoram’s credit are antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral properties, and it even has mild sedative properties, which is why it’s sometimes recommended to help relieve stress and anxiety.

Not to mention, many pets enjoy the flavor of marjoram, and the extra “dose” of vitamins (including vitamins A, C, and K), minerals (iron, calcium, potassium, manganese, magnesium, and zinc), and antioxidants (beta-carotene, zeaxanthin, lutein, and more) are just the icing on the proverbial cake.

Fresh rosemary is also an excellent option to use in these homemade treats (as pictured). Unfortunately, rosemary has come under undo fire in the last 15 years since it’s been a common addition to pet foods as a natural preservative. Human literature states people with epilepsy should avoid high levels of rosemary oil, and this has translated into pet parents assuming this amazing herb causes seizures, which is absolutely does not.

Not only is there no reason to fear giving this medicinal herb to your pets, it’s a wonderful all-natural source of iron, calcium, and vitamin B6, which is critical for healthy neurologic wellbeing.

Really, very few store-bought treats can compare to the nutrition and flavor found in homemade pet treats. Your pets will certainly adore you for making them, and they make thoughtful gifts for your pet-loving friends and family too.

  • 2 Herb Knowledge, Marjoram

item.title: They Might Love You More Than Their Favorite Treat
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • When dogs were shown human images while in an MRI scanner, activity increased in the temporal cortex region of the brain
  • The temporal cortex is used to process complex stimuli like faces in humans and, apparently, also in dogs
  • Human images, but not images of inanimate objects, also led to increased activity in the caudate brain region, which is involved in reward processes
  • This suggests that dogs found viewing human faces to be more rewarding than viewing inanimate objects
  • Dogs are not simply chowhounds — they’re social creatures who appear to enjoy spending time with their owners just as much, if not more so, than a good meal

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published November 21, 2016.

Have you ever wished you could read your dog’s mind? What is really going through his head when he greets you at the front door, doggy smiles, sloppy kisses, tail wagging and all?

Well now you can, at least to some extent, thanks to an intriguing study by researchers from the University of Mexico.1 It’s well-known that dogs relate socially to humans and have for thousands of years.

Dogs recognize their owners’ faces and pay close attention to their cues in order to gauge their emotions.

In humans, brain regions exist that help process other human faces much in this same way, and the researchers wanted to find out if similar brain regions exist in dogs.

Your Dog May Visually Process Human Faces the Way You Do

The study involved seven dogs (five border collies, one golden retriever and one Labrador retriever), which were first trained to remain awake, still and unrestrained inside an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scanner.

While in the MRI, the dogs were then shown 50 images of humans and 50 images of everyday inanimate objects. When the dogs saw human images, activity increased in the temporal cortex region of the brain.

The temporal cortex is part of the ventral visual pathway and is used to process complex stimuli like faces, in humans and, apparently, also in dogs.

What this suggests is that viewing human faces triggers the same brain regions — those used to process facial cues — in both humans and dogs. The human images also led to increased activity in subcortical structures like the caudate, which is involved in reward processes.

This suggests that, as you’d imagine, dogs found viewing the human faces to be more rewarding than viewing inanimate objects.2 The thalamus also showed increased activity when dogs were shown photos of human faces; this brain area has been related in humans to an emotional response toward faces.3

Dogs Have a Remarkable Ability to ‘Read Your Mind’

Dogs are uniquely integrated into humans’ social structures, making them a perfect choice to study social cognition. As the researchers noted, “they possess unique cognitive skills that make them more similar to a human infant than other species.”4

For instance, dogs can discriminate between two human faces, even if they’re similar.

“… [T]he detail of the information that a dog can acquire from a mere glimpse towards a human face, even without training, is extraordinary,” the researchers continued, noting that dogs have a “remarkable ability” to pick up on small signals indicating a person’s mind frame.

Your dog can, for example, tell when you’re smiling or in a neutral state, as well as when you’re paying him attention and when you’re not (and may be more likely to ask for food from a person he can establish eye contact with).

Other intriguing “dog habits” include the tendency to look at an unfamiliar human face longer than a familiar one, as well as pay less attention to his owner if his head is covered. According to the researchers:5

“This tendency to look at a human face during interaction has not been found in other canids, not even in extremely socialized wolves. Altogether, these findings show that dogs are capable of perceiving subtle traits in human faces and that they use this information to modulate their behavior.”

This makes perfect sense, as a dog’s ability to recognize and respond to human facial cues may be crucial for its survival.

As the study noted, some dogs may have more contact with human faces than they do with other dog’s faces, so perhaps that’s why they are able to recognize human facial cues without any training while other canids, like wolves, likely cannot.

Proof That Dogs Love Their Humans?

Other research on dogs’ brain activity, and in particular the “reward center” or caudate nucleus, has also revealed fascinating insights into dogs’ emotional capacity.

The caudate plays a role in human anticipation of enjoyable things (like food and love) and is activated accordingly. Previous research by Emory University neuroscientist Dr. Gregory Berns and colleagues revealed remarkable similarities in caudate activation in dogs.

Activity increased in response to hand signals indicating food, the return of an owner who had stepped out of sight and other scenarios that would similarly activate the caudate in humans. Berns wrote in The New York Times:6

“Do these findings prove that dogs love us? Not quite. But many of the same things that activate the human caudate, which are associated with positive emotions, also activate the dog caudate. Neuroscientists call this a functional homology, and it may be an indication of canine emotions.
The ability to experience positive emotions, like love and attachment, would mean that dogs have a level of sentience comparable to that of a human child. And this ability suggests a rethinking of how we treat dogs.”

If you’re a dog lover you already know that your dog is a thinking, sentient creature, but in case there was any doubt, one of the most revealing studies to date looked into whether a dog would willingly choose to receive a food treat or praise from its owner.7

You might assume a dog would gobble up a treat over praise any day, but the study actually found the opposite.

Most of the dogs preferred praise over food or liked both equally, which suggests dogs are not simply chowhounds — they’re social creatures who appear to enjoy spending time with their owners just as much, if not more so, than a good meal.

Sources and References

  • 1,3,4,5 PLOS One March 2, 2016
  • 2 IFL Science March 4, 2016
  • 6 The New York Times October 6, 2013
  • 7 Social, Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience July 7, 2016

item.title: Get Ready for Seasonal Allergies — Take These Steps Now
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Seasonal allergies in dogs and cats typically manifest in the skin rather than the eyes and respiratory tract, as in the case of human allergies
  • Pets with seasonal allergies are typically very itchy, and the itch-scratch cycle creates irritated, inflamed skin, hot spots, and secondary infections
  • There are many steps you can take, starting now, to relieve your pet’s seasonal discomfort, including addressing the diet, treating leaky gut syndrome if it is diagnosed, and providing essential fatty acid supplementation
  • It’s also important to minimize indoor allergens in your home, and when spring arrives, give your pet regular foot soaks, baths and eye rinses
  • In consultation with your integrative veterinarian, give your dog or cat natural antihistamines, and if necessary, consider a desensitization protocol ideally instituted before the start of allergy season

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 1, 2020.

Spring will arrive before long, and so will those miserable warm weather allergies so many pets suffer from these days. If you also deal with seasonal allergies, chances are you sniffle and sneeze, your eyes are itchy and watery, and you may develop an irritating cough, some shortness of breath or even difficulty breathing.

These are all very common human symptoms of allergies, but strangely enough, if your dog or cat has a seasonal allergic response, it will most often manifest as a condition called allergic dermatitis, which is irritation or inflammation of the skin. It's rare that a dog or cat develops symptoms similar to those of an allergic human.

Just to clarify, there are two main categories of allergies — food and environmental. Food allergies create year-round symptoms in pets, whereas seasonal environmental allergy symptoms flare intermittently depending on when triggers bloom, blossom and grow.

Sensitivities to dust mites or fleas are environmental triggers that can be year-round, depending on your pet's exposure.

Telltale Signs of Seasonal Allergies in Pets

  • Intense itchiness — Dogs and cats with allergies are usually very itchy. They scratch at themselves and may show signs of irritability. Some might bite or chew at a specific area of the body, while others are itchy from nose to tail. You may catch your pet rubbing his body against your furniture or along the carpet to help relieve that miserable itch.
  • Hair loss and skin issues — As the itch-scratch cycle worsens, the skin becomes inflamed and tender, which can set the stage for secondary infections. There might also be areas of hair loss and open or crusty sores, including hot spots — areas of inflamed, infected skin resulting from an overgrowth of normal skin bacteria.
  • Problems with the ears and feet — Pets with seasonal allergies typically have issues with their ears and feet. The ear canals become itchy and inflamed, and they often become infected with yeast or bacteria. Symptoms of an ear infection include scratching at the ears, head shaking, hair loss around the ears, and a bad smell or discharge coming from the ears.

    Because dogs and cats sweat from the pads of their feet, when they go outside, allergens cling to their paws. Those allergens get tracked back inside and all around your home, especially in areas where your pet hangs out, and are a major source of itchiness.

    Allergic pets often lick or chew at their paws and toes. The excessive licking and chewing can spark a secondary yeast infection, so if your pet's feet start smelling musty, or like cheese popcorn or corn chips, chances are she's developed a yeast infection.
  • Respiratory symptoms — Although it's not common, some pets, especially cats, can develop symptoms similar to those of an allergic human, such as a runny nose, watery eyes, sneezing, and coughing.

Seasonal Allergies Often Progress to Year-Round Allergies

Allergic reactions are produced by your pet's immune system, and the way her immune system functions is a result of both nature (genetics) and nurture (environment). Some variation of the following history is often seen with allergic pets:

  • A young pup or kitten, 4 to 6 months old, begins with a little red tummy, itchy ears, and a mild infection in one ear. His regular veterinarian treats him symptomatically — often with a round of unnecessary antibiotics — to appease the owner. Believe it or not, this is enough to set the stage for leaky gut.
  • The following year as soon as the weather warms up, the pet is brought back to his regular vet with very itchy feet, another ear infection, and a hotspot or two. Again, the vet treats the symptoms (sadly, often with steroids) until the weather turns cold and the symptoms disappear.
  • Year three, the same pet suffers from May through September with red, inflamed skin, some hair loss, more hotspots, frequent ear and skin infections, and a tendency to chew his paws or scratch until he bleeds.
  • By year five, all the symptoms have grown significantly worse and the animal's suffering is now year-round.

This is what commonly happens with seasonal environmental allergies. The more your pet is exposed to the allergens he's sensitive to, the more intense and long-lasting his allergic response becomes. That's why it's extremely important to begin addressing potential root causes at the first sign of an allergic response, no matter how mild it appears at its onset.

How to Help a Pet with Allergies

The following are common sense, all-natural steps you can take to help ease your allergic pet's discomfort. Many can be implemented right away, before spring, to give your dog or cat a leg up once allergy season arrives.

If you know your pet has seasonal allergies, it’s best not to wait until symptoms occur to start an allergy protocol. Preventing systemic inflammation is a whole lot easier than addressing a profound allergic response, once it's occurring.

  1. Address the diet — One of the first things to do for a dog or cat with allergies is to review their diet and check for leaky gut syndrome (dysbiosis), which is often the reason seasonal allergies get progressively worse from one year to the next.

    Your pet's gastrointestinal (GI) tract has the very important job of deciding what nutrients to allow into the bloodstream, and which to keep out. The job of the GI tract is to allow nutrients in while keeping allergens out. When the gut starts to "leak," it means it's allowing allergens into the bloodstream.

    Often medications, especially antibiotics and steroids, cause leaky gut syndrome. Any pet on routine drug therapy should be assessed for a leaky gut. Another trigger for leaky gut is a processed diet containing genetically modified ingredients.

    There's a canine microbiota dysbiosis test from the Texas A&M GI lab you can use to check for this condition. Even better, have your pet's microbiome assessed through AnimalBiome. They also have a biome restoration program that can dramatically improve pet's quality of life.

    Pets with allergies should be transitioned to an anti-inflammatory diet very low in starch content (less than 15%). It should contain no soy, corn, rice, wheat, organic whole wheat, tapioca, peas, lentils, chickpeas, or potatoes. By eliminating extra sugar and carbohydrates in the diet, you'll also limit the food supply for yeast, which can be very beneficial for allergic pets.

    It's also important to offer your pet clean, pure drinking water that doesn't contain fluoride, fluorine, heavy metals, or other contaminants.
  2. Supplement essential fatty acids (EFA) and lauric acid — Boosting the omega-3 fatty acids in your allergic pet’s diet is recommended. The best sources of these fatty acids come from the ocean, including krill, salmon, tuna, anchovy, and sardine oil, and other sources of fish body oils. Phytoplankton does not contain enough omega-3 fatty acids to moderate allergic inflammatory responses or meet minimum EFA requirements for dogs and cats.

    Coconut oil is also recommended for allergic pets because it contains lauric acid, which has natural antifungal properties that can help suppress the production of yeast in the body. Omega-3 oils combined with coconut oil can modulate or even suppress the inflammatory response in allergic pets.
  3. Refuse all unnecessary vaccines, pest preventives, and veterinary drugs — Because allergies are an exaggerated immune system response, it's important to avoid unnecessary vaccines and veterinary drugs, including chemical pest preventives, all of which interfere with the performance of the immune system.

    If your pet is taking medication regularly or has taken a long-term course of medication in the past, talk to your veterinarian about instituting an intermittent detoxification protocol to help the body eliminate harmful byproducts and drug residues.
  4. Minimize indoor allergens — Another thing you can do to help your allergic pet is reduce allergens and toxins around your home. Vacuum all carpets, rugs, and upholstery, clean hard floors, and wash pet and human bedding in natural, fragrance-free detergent a minimum of once a week. Don't use dryer sheets.

    Keep the areas of your home where your pet spends most of her time as allergen-free as possible. Use nontoxic cleaning agents instead of traditional household cleaners.

    During allergy season, keep windows closed as much as possible, and change the filters on your heating or air circulation unit often. Invest in an air purifier to remove allergens inside the house. Also consider covering your pet's bed with a dust mite cover that can be frequently washed to help reduce allergen contamination that she may be bringing in from outside.

    Eliminating all chemical air scenting products such as plug ins, scented candles, room sprays and pet odor sprays that contain toxic ingredients is also recommended.
  5. Rinse your pet regularly and do daily foot soaks and eye rinses — Once the warm weather arrives, one of the best things you can do is help rid your pet's body of allergens. Dogs and cats who are outside regularly collect millions of allergens. It's just common sense to rinse them off, which can provide immediate relief for irritated, inflamed skin.

    When it’s time to actually bathe pets (when they’re stinky, dirty or have a skin infection), it’s recommended to use only grain-free and pH balanced shampoos. Because oatmeal is a carbohydrate and carbs feed yeast, oatmeal shampoos aren’t recommended. Follow up with a lemon juice or vinegar rinse to help manage yeast infections.

    If your pet has been prescribed a medicated shampoo, rebalancing the skin's microbiome is a wise idea: mix a teaspoon of probiotic powder in a quart of water and pour over your pet from the neck to the tail, rub in and towel dry.

    Foot soaks are a great way to reduce the number of allergens your pet tracks into the house and deposits all over her indoor environment.

    Daily eye rinses can also be very effective for pets who are pawing at their eyes. It's very important that you not use human medicated eye drops. There's a great all-natural over-the-counter eye drop that's made by Halo Pets that can reduce eye irritation and inflammation. Colloidal silver is also a great way to safely disinfect your pet's face and delicate areas around the eyes.
  6. Give natural antihistamines — There are supplements commonly prescribed for pets with seasonal allergic issues, starting with quercetin, which is a bioflavonoid with anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antihistamine properties. Quercetin is often called “nature’s Benadryl,” because it’s very effective at suppressing histamine release.

    Bromelain and papain are proteolytic enzymes that increase absorption of quercetin, making it more effective. Bromelain and papain are often combined with vitamin C and quercetin, because they have a great synergistic effect. It’s recommended to start this protocol with an allergic pet several weeks before the weather begins to warm up or a month before your pet normally shows allergy symptoms.

    Herbs such as stinging nettle, butterbur, sorrel, verbena, elderflower, and cat's claw have a documented history of helping animals combat seasonal allergic responses.

    Plant sterols and sterolins, which are anti-inflammatory agents, have also been used successfully to modulate the immune system toward a more balanced response in allergic patients. Immune-modulating supplements, such as arabinogalactans, can also be beneficial.

    Locally produced honey contains a small amount of pollen from the local area that can help desensitize the body to local allergens over time. Usually the best place to find local honey is at a farmer's market or neighborhood health food store. Check with your veterinarian about the right dose for your dog or cat.

    Most importantly, begin a seasonal allergy support protocol before your pet becomes itchy, red and inflamed. Waiting until your pet becomes miserable makes it difficult to get through allergy season without using allergy drugs that have side effects.

    Instituting a natural support protocol before allergy season commences means you have the potential to moderate your animal's histamine production, which can result in milder symptoms and a less itchy pet.
  7. Consider a desensitization protocol — If you've tried the above suggestions with limited success, consider helping your pet’s immune system quiet down through desensitization. This can be achieved through a technique called Nambudripad's Allergy Elimination Techniques (NAET) performed by practitioners trained to treat dogs and cats, or through sublingual immunotherapy.

    Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) is a variation on allergy injections to treat atopic dermatitis (skin allergies) in dogs, cats, and horses. SLIT is common in Europe and is used to treat respiratory and skin allergies in people. Sublingual immunotherapy is given orally, which is much easier on both you and your pet than injections.

    Good success has been seen with a sublingual product called regionally-specific immunotherapy, or RESPIT®. It’s favored because it doesn’t rely on testing to determine what your dog or cat is allergic to. It uses a mixture of the most significant regional allergens instead.

    If you decide to try sublingual immunotherapy, it's important to know that most pets require an "immediate relief" protocol (including therapeutic bathing, herbs and nutraceuticals that reduce inflammation), in addition to beginning a desensitization protocol of any kind.

    Desensitizing pets is one of the best long-term solutions for managing allergies, and sublingual immunotherapy is a needle-free option.

  • It’s also important to minimize indoor allergens in your home, and when spring arrives, give your pet regular foot soaks, baths and eye rinses
  • In consultation with your integrative veterinarian, give your dog or cat natural antihistamines, and if necessary, consider a desensitization protocol ideally instituted before the start of allergy season

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 1, 2020.

Spring will arrive before long, and so will those miserable warm weather allergies so many pets suffer from these days. If you also deal with seasonal allergies, chances are you sniffle and sneeze, your eyes are itchy and watery, and you may develop an irritating cough, some shortness of breath or even difficulty breathing.

These are all very common human symptoms of allergies, but strangely enough, if your dog or cat has a seasonal allergic response, it will most often manifest as a condition called allergic dermatitis, which is irritation or inflammation of the skin. It's rare that a dog or cat develops symptoms similar to those of an allergic human.

Just to clarify, there are two main categories of allergies — food and environmental. Food allergies create year-round symptoms in pets, whereas seasonal environmental allergy symptoms flare intermittently depending on when triggers bloom, blossom and grow.

Sensitivities to dust mites or fleas are environmental triggers that can be year-round, depending on your pet's exposure.

Telltale Signs of Seasonal Allergies in Pets

  • Intense itchiness — Dogs and cats with allergies are usually very itchy. They scratch at themselves and may show signs of irritability. Some might bite or chew at a specific area of the body, while others are itchy from nose to tail. You may catch your pet rubbing his body against your furniture or along the carpet to help relieve that miserable itch.
  • Hair loss and skin issues — As the itch-scratch cycle worsens, the skin becomes inflamed and tender, which can set the stage for secondary infections. There might also be areas of hair loss and open or crusty sores, including hot spots — areas of inflamed, infected skin resulting from an overgrowth of normal skin bacteria.
  • Problems with the ears and feet — Pets with seasonal allergies typically have issues with their ears and feet. The ear canals become itchy and inflamed, and they often become infected with yeast or bacteria. Symptoms of an ear infection include scratching at the ears, head shaking, hair loss around the ears, and a bad smell or discharge coming from the ears.

    Because dogs and cats sweat from the pads of their feet, when they go outside, allergens cling to their paws. Those allergens get tracked back inside and all around your home, especially in areas where your pet hangs out, and are a major source of itchiness.

    Allergic pets often lick or chew at their paws and toes. The excessive licking and chewing can spark a secondary yeast infection, so if your pet's feet start smelling musty, or like cheese popcorn or corn chips, chances are she's developed a yeast infection.
  • Respiratory symptoms — Although it's not common, some pets, especially cats, can develop symptoms similar to those of an allergic human, such as a runny nose, watery eyes, sneezing, and coughing.

Seasonal Allergies Often Progress to Year-Round Allergies

Allergic reactions are produced by your pet's immune system, and the way her immune system functions is a result of both nature (genetics) and nurture (environment). Some variation of the following history is often seen with allergic pets:

  • A young pup or kitten, 4 to 6 months old, begins with a little red tummy, itchy ears, and a mild infection in one ear. His regular veterinarian treats him symptomatically — often with a round of unnecessary antibiotics — to appease the owner. Believe it or not, this is enough to set the stage for leaky gut.
  • The following year as soon as the weather warms up, the pet is brought back to his regular vet with very itchy feet, another ear infection, and a hotspot or two. Again, the vet treats the symptoms (sadly, often with steroids) until the weather turns cold and the symptoms disappear.
  • Year three, the same pet suffers from May through September with red, inflamed skin, some hair loss, more hotspots, frequent ear and skin infections, and a tendency to chew his paws or scratch until he bleeds.
  • By year five, all the symptoms have grown significantly worse and the animal's suffering is now year-round.

This is what commonly happens with seasonal environmental allergies. The more your pet is exposed to the allergens he's sensitive to, the more intense and long-lasting his allergic response becomes. That's why it's extremely important to begin addressing potential root causes at the first sign of an allergic response, no matter how mild it appears at its onset.

How to Help a Pet with Allergies

The following are common sense, all-natural steps you can take to help ease your allergic pet's discomfort. Many can be implemented right away, before spring, to give your dog or cat a leg up once allergy season arrives.

If you know your pet has seasonal allergies, it’s best not to wait until symptoms occur to start an allergy protocol. Preventing systemic inflammation is a whole lot easier than addressing a profound allergic response, once it's occurring.

  1. Address the diet — One of the first things to do for a dog or cat with allergies is to review their diet and check for leaky gut syndrome (dysbiosis), which is often the reason seasonal allergies get progressively worse from one year to the next.

    Your pet's gastrointestinal (GI) tract has the very important job of deciding what nutrients to allow into the bloodstream, and which to keep out. The job of the GI tract is to allow nutrients in while keeping allergens out. When the gut starts to "leak," it means it's allowing allergens into the bloodstream.

    Often medications, especially antibiotics and steroids, cause leaky gut syndrome. Any pet on routine drug therapy should be assessed for a leaky gut. Another trigger for leaky gut is a processed diet containing genetically modified ingredients.

    There's a canine microbiota dysbiosis test from the Texas A&M GI lab you can use to check for this condition. Even better, have your pet's microbiome assessed through AnimalBiome. They also have a biome restoration program that can dramatically improve pet's quality of life.

    Pets with allergies should be transitioned to an anti-inflammatory diet very low in starch content (less than 15%). It should contain no soy, corn, rice, wheat, organic whole wheat, tapioca, peas, lentils, chickpeas, or potatoes. By eliminating extra sugar and carbohydrates in the diet, you'll also limit the food supply for yeast, which can be very beneficial for allergic pets.

    It's also important to offer your pet clean, pure drinking water that doesn't contain fluoride, fluorine, heavy metals, or other contaminants.
  2. Supplement essential fatty acids (EFA) and lauric acid — Boosting the omega-3 fatty acids in your allergic pet’s diet is recommended. The best sources of these fatty acids come from the ocean, including krill, salmon, tuna, anchovy, and sardine oil, and other sources of fish body oils. Phytoplankton does not contain enough omega-3 fatty acids to moderate allergic inflammatory responses or meet minimum EFA requirements for dogs and cats.

    Coconut oil is also recommended for allergic pets because it contains lauric acid, which has natural antifungal properties that can help suppress the production of yeast in the body. Omega-3 oils combined with coconut oil can modulate or even suppress the inflammatory response in allergic pets.
  3. Refuse all unnecessary vaccines, pest preventives, and veterinary drugs — Because allergies are an exaggerated immune system response, it's important to avoid unnecessary vaccines and veterinary drugs, including chemical pest preventives, all of which interfere with the performance of the immune system.

    If your pet is taking medication regularly or has taken a long-term course of medication in the past, talk to your veterinarian about instituting an intermittent detoxification protocol to help the body eliminate harmful byproducts and drug residues.
  4. Minimize indoor allergens — Another thing you can do to help your allergic pet is reduce allergens and toxins around your home. Vacuum all carpets, rugs, and upholstery, clean hard floors, and wash pet and human bedding in natural, fragrance-free detergent a minimum of once a week. Don't use dryer sheets.

    Keep the areas of your home where your pet spends most of her time as allergen-free as possible. Use nontoxic cleaning agents instead of traditional household cleaners.

    During allergy season, keep windows closed as much as possible, and change the filters on your heating or air circulation unit often. Invest in an air purifier to remove allergens inside the house. Also consider covering your pet's bed with a dust mite cover that can be frequently washed to help reduce allergen contamination that she may be bringing in from outside.

    Eliminating all chemical air scenting products such as plug ins, scented candles, room sprays and pet odor sprays that contain toxic ingredients is also recommended.
  5. Rinse your pet regularly and do daily foot soaks and eye rinses — Once the warm weather arrives, one of the best things you can do is help rid your pet's body of allergens. Dogs and cats who are outside regularly collect millions of allergens. It's just common sense to rinse them off, which can provide immediate relief for irritated, inflamed skin.

    When it’s time to actually bathe pets (when they’re stinky, dirty or have a skin infection), it’s recommended to use only grain-free and pH balanced shampoos. Because oatmeal is a carbohydrate and carbs feed yeast, oatmeal shampoos aren’t recommended. Follow up with a lemon juice or vinegar rinse to help manage yeast infections.

    If your pet has been prescribed a medicated shampoo, rebalancing the skin's microbiome is a wise idea: mix a teaspoon of probiotic powder in a quart of water and pour over your pet from the neck to the tail, rub in and towel dry.

    Foot soaks are a great way to reduce the number of allergens your pet tracks into the house and deposits all over her indoor environment.

    Daily eye rinses can also be very effective for pets who are pawing at their eyes. It's very important that you not use human medicated eye drops. There's a great all-natural over-the-counter eye drop that's made by Halo Pets that can reduce eye irritation and inflammation. Colloidal silver is also a great way to safely disinfect your pet's face and delicate areas around the eyes.
  6. Give natural antihistamines — There are supplements commonly prescribed for pets with seasonal allergic issues, starting with quercetin, which is a bioflavonoid with anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antihistamine properties. Quercetin is often called “nature’s Benadryl,” because it’s very effective at suppressing histamine release.

    Bromelain and papain are proteolytic enzymes that increase absorption of quercetin, making it more effective. Bromelain and papain are often combined with vitamin C and quercetin, because they have a great synergistic effect. It’s recommended to start this protocol with an allergic pet several weeks before the weather begins to warm up or a month before your pet normally shows allergy symptoms.

    Herbs such as stinging nettle, butterbur, sorrel, verbena, elderflower, and cat's claw have a documented history of helping animals combat seasonal allergic responses.

    Plant sterols and sterolins, which are anti-inflammatory agents, have also been used successfully to modulate the immune system toward a more balanced response in allergic patients. Immune-modulating supplements, such as arabinogalactans, can also be beneficial.

    Locally produced honey contains a small amount of pollen from the local area that can help desensitize the body to local allergens over time. Usually the best place to find local honey is at a farmer's market or neighborhood health food store. Check with your veterinarian about the right dose for your dog or cat.

    Most importantly, begin a seasonal allergy support protocol before your pet becomes itchy, red and inflamed. Waiting until your pet becomes miserable makes it difficult to get through allergy season without using allergy drugs that have side effects.

    Instituting a natural support protocol before allergy season commences means you have the potential to moderate your animal's histamine production, which can result in milder symptoms and a less itchy pet.
  7. Consider a desensitization protocol — If you've tried the above suggestions with limited success, consider helping your pet’s immune system quiet down through desensitization. This can be achieved through a technique called Nambudripad's Allergy Elimination Techniques (NAET) performed by practitioners trained to treat dogs and cats, or through sublingual immunotherapy.

    Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) is a variation on allergy injections to treat atopic dermatitis (skin allergies) in dogs, cats, and horses. SLIT is common in Europe and is used to treat respiratory and skin allergies in people. Sublingual immunotherapy is given orally, which is much easier on both you and your pet than injections.

    Good success has been seen with a sublingual product called regionally-specific immunotherapy, or RESPIT®. It’s favored because it doesn’t rely on testing to determine what your dog or cat is allergic to. It uses a mixture of the most significant regional allergens instead.

    If you decide to try sublingual immunotherapy, it's important to know that most pets require an "immediate relief" protocol (including therapeutic bathing, herbs and nutraceuticals that reduce inflammation), in addition to beginning a desensitization protocol of any kind.

    Desensitizing pets is one of the best long-term solutions for managing allergies, and sublingual immunotherapy is a needle-free option.

item.title: When the Paw Licking Just Won't Quit
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The warm, moist, poorly ventilated spaces between a dog's toes are a natural haven for Malassezia yeast and Staphylococcus bacteria, both of which live harmlessly on skin until conditions let them multiply
  • Chronic paw licking usually signals allergies, not the main problem. Inflammation disrupts the skin barrier, and constant licking then macerates the tissue further, driving a self-perpetuating cycle
  • Paw soak options range from gentle to strong: plain water rinses, cooled herbal teas, apple cider vinegar with green or chamomile tea, diluted white vinegar, povidone-iodine, and chlorhexidine for confirmed mixed infections
  • Thorough drying after every soak is non-negotiable. Moisture trapped between the toes feeds the exact organisms you're trying to eliminate, so a good towel and even a cool blow dryer are essential
  • Real resolution comes from addressing the root cause: a clean, species-appropriate diet, gut support, environmental awareness, and working with an integrative vet on the deeper allergy or immune story driving recurrent flare-ups

It usually starts as a quiet, little slurping sound in the background. You look over, and there's your dog, hunched over one paw, going at it like they're trying to shine a shoe. You call their name, and they stop for a second, but as soon as you look away, they start again.

If you've noticed your dog licking, chewing, or biting at their paws, sometimes so obsessively that it keeps you awake at night, there's a very good chance something is going on between those toes that they can't tell you about. Thankfully, gentle at-home approaches can provide real relief while you and your vet address the underlying cause.

Why Paws Are a Perfect Storm

The spaces between a dog's toes are warm, dark, poorly ventilated, and constantly picking up moisture from walking on grass, sidewalks, puddles, snow, wet lawns, and floors your dog has just wandered across. That microenvironment is basically a petri dish. Two organisms in particular love these conditions: the Malassezia pachydermatis yeast and the Staphylococcus pseudintermedius bacteria.

Both naturally live on dog skin, and in small numbers, they're harmless. But give them warmth, moisture, and a disrupted skin barrier, and they multiply fast.1 Dogs with tight interdigital webbing, hairy feet, or heavy skin folds around the paws are especially vulnerable. So are dogs who swim, run through wet grass, or come home from walks with damp feet that never quite dry out.

The Underlying Cause Most Owners Miss

Most integrative and holistic veterinarians believe paw yeast and bacterial infections are almost always symptoms of something else. The most common something else is allergies. When a dog with atopic dermatitis or food sensitivity walks on grass, carpet, or any allergen-laden surface, the immune system fires off an inflammatory response in the paw skin. That inflammation disrupts the natural skin barrier, changes local pH, and shifts the composition of the skin's protective secretions — all of which create conditions where yeast and bacteria flourish.2,3

Licking makes it worse: Saliva deposits moisture and digestive enzymes on the skin, further macerating the tissue and cranking up the humidity between the toes. Damp, damaged skin is even more hospitable to microbes. More microbes mean more itching, and more itching means more licking — the cycle continues.

From a holistic perspective, chasing the surface infection with soak after soak without addressing what drives the inflammation keeps you in the loop indefinitely. The soaks matter. But so does the root cause.

Signs to Watch For

Early recognition means earlier intervention. The tricky part is that paw problems often start subtly and only get labeled a "problem" when they're impossible to ignore — so learning the earliest hints buys you time to intervene before things escalate. Common signs of a paw yeast or bacterial issue include:4

  • Obsessive licking, chewing, or biting at the paws
  • A distinctive musty, corn-chip, or yeasty smell coming from the feet
  • Reddish-brown saliva staining on light-colored fur between the toes
  • Redness, swelling, or puffiness in the interdigital spaces
  • Greasy, waxy, or crusty debris around the paw pads and nail beds
  • Limping or reluctance to walk on hard surfaces
  • Thickened, darkened, elephant-skin texture in chronic cases
  • Frequent ear issues alongside the paw problem; a classic clue that allergies are in the mix

Which Dogs Get Hit Hardest

Some breeds are just built for this problem. If your dog is one of these, a proactive paw care routine is worth building into daily life:

  • English Bulldogs — They have broad, flat paws, tight interdigital spaces, and heavy skin folds that trap moisture.
  • Labrador Retrievers — One of the most allergy-prone breeds, plus they love water, which keeps their paws damp.
  • Cocker Spaniels — Their heavily feathered paws hold moisture against the skin.
  • West Highland White Terriers — They have a high rate of atopic dermatitis, and their white fur shows every stain.
  • Basset Hounds — They have large, heavy paws, deep interdigital folds, and low-slung bodies that keep feet close to damp ground.

However, keep in mind that any dog with allergies, even breeds not on this list, can still get stuck in the same cycle.

Paw Soak Options: From Gentle to Strong

Paw soaks are one of the most effective at-home tools for interdigital problems because they deliver treatment directly into the spaces sprays and wipes can't reach. Here are the options integrative and holistic veterinarians most often reach for, from the gentlest to the strongest:5,6,7

  • Plain lukewarm water — A quick rinse or soak after every walk removes pollen, grass residue, dust, and other environmental material before it can trigger inflammation. This is a great daily habit even for dogs without an active problem.
  • Cooled green or chamomile tea — A gentle traditional rinse that many integrative practitioners like for mildly irritated paws. Green tea is rich in antioxidants and supports skin health, while chamomile is soothing and calming. Brew strong, cool completely, and use on intact skin. Skip if any irritation worsens.
  • Salt water — Make a simple homemade soak by dissolving 1 level teaspoon of table salt in 1 cup of previously boiled, cooled water. It helps cleanse and soothe mildly irritated but intact skin. Skip if there's cracking or raw skin, as salt stings. Never use seawater, which can contain contaminants.
  • Epsom salt — Dissolve 1 tablespoon of Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate) in a quart of warm water. It's not directly antimicrobial, but the osmotic action reduces swelling and softens crusty debris. It works well as a soothing standalone soak or as a pre-treatment before a stronger antimicrobial soak. Soak for five to 10 minutes.
  • Apple cider vinegar and herbal tea — Mix 4 cups warm water with 1 to 2 tablespoons raw, unfiltered apple cider vinegar (with the mother) and 1 cup strongly brewed, cooled green or chamomile tea. It works best for itchy, yeast-prone, or allergy-affected paws.

    Soak for three to five minutes, then pat dry thoroughly without rinsing. Some conventional vets prefer distilled white vinegar over ACV, arguing that the organic compounds in cider vinegar could feed yeast. Both camps have their reasoning. Watch how your dog's paws respond and follow what works.
  • Diluted white vinegar — Mix one part distilled white vinegar with two to four parts water for a mildly acidic soak (pH around 3 to 4) that inhibits yeast growth. Malassezia yeast thrives in alkaline environments, so acidifying the skin surface disrupts its growth cycle. This is ideal for mild yeast overgrowth or as a maintenance soak. However, never use it on broken or raw skin — the acidity will sting. Soak for five minutes, then pat dry.
  • Povidone-iodine (Betadine) — Both conventional and holistic veterinarians widely recommend this for more inflamed or infected paws. Add just enough povidone-iodine to warm water so the solution turns the color of weak iced tea or light amber. Soak for 2 to 5 minutes and pat dry; no rinsing needed. Iodine has strong antifungal and antibacterial action.

    However, do not use this daily long-term, on deep wounds, extensively broken skin, or on dogs with known iodine sensitivity. It can also temporarily stain light fur, which is cosmetic and harmless.
  • Chlorhexidine — This is the strongest of the commonly used soaks. Dilute a 2% chlorhexidine gluconate stock solution to a 0.05% working strength (about 1 ounce per 40 ounces of lukewarm water) until the solution turns pale blue-green. This broad-spectrum works against both yeast and bacteria, with residual binding activity that keeps working for hours after the soak.

    Soak for five to 10 minutes and don't rinse; the residual layer is part of the benefit. It works best for confirmed mixed yeast and bacterial infections, ideally guided by a veterinary cytology sample.

How to Actually Do a Paw Soak

The setup is simpler than it sounds. Most pet parents picture something elaborate and end up putting it off entirely, but a paw soak is really just a shallow container of the right solution, a few minutes of your dog's cooperation, and a good towel at the end. Here's the basic flow:

  • Choose your container: a shallow basin for small dogs, a shower tray or bathtub for larger dogs, or a bucket if that's what you have.
  • Fill it with enough solution to cover the paw pads and interdigital spaces (usually 2 to 3 inches deep).
  • Use lukewarm water, never hot.
  • Place the paw in and gently spread the toes so the solution reaches every crevice.
  • Follow the recommended time for whichever soak you're using.
  • Pat completely dry with a clean towel, spreading the toes to blot the webbing.
  • For heavy paw fur, a cool-setting hair dryer held 12 inches away helps ensure complete drying.

Take note that the drying step is not optional. Moisture trapped between the toes after a soak feeds exactly the organisms you're trying to eliminate. Skipping this step can actually make things worse.

If your dog resists sitting in a basin, try a lick mat spread with a little peanut butter (xylitol-free) at nose height to distract them. Some pet parents soak one paw at a time in a smaller container while the dog lies on their side. A large zip-lock bag held around the ankle also works in a pinch.

Frequency depends on what you're treating. Mild seasonal irritation might need a soak or rinse one to three times a week. An active infection might need daily soaks for one to two weeks, then every other day for two weeks, then a maintenance rhythm of two to three times a week. Work with your vet to dial it in.

Beyond the Soak, Address the Real Problem

Paw soaks treat the surface, but real resolution requires looking at what's driving the inflammation and infection in the first place. From an integrative and holistic point of view, the questions worth asking include:

  • What's going into the bowl? Food is often the biggest overlooked factor in chronic skin problems. Grains, starches, additives, preservatives, and highly processed ingredients can all contribute to inflammation and immune irritation. Many holistic vets start with a clean, species-appropriate whole-food diet and careful attention to every treat, chew, supplement, and flavored medication. Sometimes progress begins with what you take out, not what you add.
  • How's the gut? Gut health has an outsized influence on skin. A disrupted microbiome shows up in the skin barrier, in inflammation levels, and in how well the immune system tolerates environmental triggers. Supporting the gut is often the missing link in stubborn skin cases.
  • What's the environment doing? Grasses, pollen, dust mites, mold, damp conditions, new carpets, floor cleaners, fragranced household products, lawn treatments, and glyphosate-sprayed grass can all contribute. You can't eliminate every trigger, but noticing patterns like whether it's worse after certain walks, in certain seasons, or after certain products go on the floor can give you real leverage.
  • What's the daily maintenance? Simple habits change outcomes, such as:

    • • Keeping a designated paw towel by every door and wiping paws after every outing
    • • Trimming the fur between paw pads and toes so the skin can breathe and dry
    • • Washing and drying pet bedding weekly to reduce allergen buildup
    • • Rinsing paws after walks in areas with lawn chemicals or heavy pollen
    • • Considering a paw balm or plain aloe vera product for dry intact skin
    For dogs prone to recurrent issues, a preventive maintenance soak two to three times a week keeps microbial populations below the threshold that triggers symptoms.

When to Call the Vet

Home care has real value, but some situations need veterinary attention. Skip the soak and get to the vet if:

  • Paws are painful, hot, or causing limping
  • There's significant swelling, cracking, ulceration, or bleeding
  • Discharge or strong odor is present
  • You see lumps or deep lesions
  • Symptoms are worsening despite home care

A cytology sample, where your vet takes a quick tape impression or swab from the interdigital skin and looks at it under a microscope, is one of the most useful tests available. It tells you whether you're dealing with yeast, bacteria, or both, and helps guide which soak makes sense for your specific situation. If soaks and standard treatments aren't working, a bacterial culture and sensitivity test can identify resistant strains like methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus pseudintermedius (MRSP), which is increasingly common and requires targeted therapy.8

If paw infections keep coming back, an allergy workup, including allergy testing, elimination diet trials, or a broader integrative assessment, is worth the investment. Managing the root cause is what breaks the cycle for good.

The Real Takeaway

A dog who won't stop licking their paws is trying to tell you something. Sometimes it's a mild seasonal irritation that a simple rinse will fix. Sometimes it's yeast, bacteria, or both, thriving in the humid space between their toes. And sometimes, it's the visible tip of a bigger allergy or dietary story that will keep resurfacing until you address it at the source.

The good news is that there's a whole ladder of at-home options that can bring meaningful relief. Layer that with thoughtful attention to diet, gut health, and environmental triggers, and with a good integrative or holistic veterinarian in your corner, most dogs can go from perpetual paw-lickers to quiet, comfortable companions again.

  • 3, 5 Raw Essentials, September 4, 2026
